sections.title: Pick a test for your goal
sections.text: A controlled push-up test reflects upper-body strength endurance, and a 30-second sit-to-stand test measures repeated lower-body function. A timed plank tests one particular kind of trunk endurance, while a step test or measured walk looks at another side of conditioning. No single test measures total fitness.

sections.title: Do it the same way every time
sections.text: Use the same push-up depth, chair height, plank position or step height, and keep the warm-up, rest and footwear similar. Stop when your technique breaks down instead of chasing a higher count. Retest after several weeks of training instead of doing max efforts every day. Write down exactly how you did each test so later comparisons mean something.

sections.title: Choose a test that fits your level
sections.text: If you’re starting from zero, you might count comfortable chair stands using a stable chair. An experienced trainee may need a harder benchmark. If a test causes pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or loss of balance, don’t use it until a professional has assessed you.

sections.title: Know the limits
sections.text: Practice, motivation, fatigue and body proportions all affect field scores. A better score may come from better skill as well as from physical change. Tests you do yourself can’t diagnose cardiovascular, neurological or musculoskeletal conditions.
